<reason>CON built a sharper structural distinction—"counting" (screen, condition, refer) versus true "parity" (labor harm can override a demonstrated price benefit)—and used it to repeatedly expose that PRO never actually defended parity's application to the decisive conflict case. The grocery-merger hypothetical, pressed in Pressure Questions and again in closing, was never resolved by PRO with a concrete decision rule; PRO's answer ("condition it," "weighed, not pre-forgiven") is functionally the same as CON's screening proposal, a point CON explicitly and correctly seized on. CON also successfully turned PRO's strongest example (hospital mergers, licensed labor) into a double-jeopardy case already caught by price-side review, and PRO's rebuttal ("merger review is the only tool that acts before scarcity is built") never squarely answered why price-side review wouldn't already block that same merger. PRO's opening mechanism and welfare-equivalence argument were compelling and its closing reframe ("CON's rule is the asymmetry restated") was rhetorically clever, but it substituted reframing for actually answering the exchange-rate challenge, leaving CON's central pressure point live and unresolved at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A4.1-A4.3 answer to Q1 (drawing the bright line between "counting/screening" and true parity, then using PRO's own B4.1 answer—"the deal proceeds on price effects alone" when the wage test shows no harm—as proof that PRO's mechanism is a screen, not parity) was the most decisive exchange; PRO's closing response reframed rather than refuted it.</best_rebuttal>
